name: Pauli exclusion principle
kicker: Why atoms have shells · No two electrons share all four quantum numbers
briefing: In 1925, the Austrian-born physicist Wolfgang Pauli found a strict rule for electrons: no two electrons in an atom can have exactly the same four quantum numbers. That means each orbital can hold only two electrons, with opposite spins, so electrons must stack into higher and higher shells, which gives the periodic table its shape. The same rule keeps dead stars called white dwarfs from collapsing under their own gravity.
answerHtml: Pauli exclusion principle (accept exclusion principle or Pauli principle; prompt on Pauli; do not accept “uncertainty principle”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: A Slater determinant automatically obeys this principle, since the determinant becomes zero whenever two electrons are put in the same state. This principle follows from the fact that swapping two identical electrons flips the sign of their combined wavefunction.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle stating that no two electrons in an atom can have the same four quantum numbers.

tossups.p: The Delta-plus-plus baryon, made of three up quarks with matching spins, seemed to break this principle until physicists gave quarks a new property called color charge. The Omega-minus, made of three strange quarks, raised the same puzzle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rule, which says that each atomic orbital can hold at most two electrons with opposite spins.

tossups.p: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar [“chun-druh-SAY-kar”] showed that a white dwarf heavier than about 1.4 times the Sun’s mass cannot be held up by the electron pressure that comes from this principle. Neutron stars are also held up by a “degeneracy pressure” that results from this principle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle stating that no two identical fermions, such as electrons, can occupy the same quantum state.

tossups.p: At absolute zero, the electrons in a metal stack up into the lowest available states until they reach a top level called the Fermi energy, instead of all crowding into the lowest state, because of this principle. Particles that obey it follow Fermi–Dirac statistics.
tossups.r: Bosons such as photons do not obey it. For 10 points, name this principle saying no two electrons in an atom can share all four quantum numbers.

tossups.p: This principle’s namesake stated it using a mysterious fourth quantum number with only two possible values, which George Uhlenbeck and Samuel Goudsmit soon identified as electron spin. That two-valued number became the spin quantum number, which is either plus one-half or minus one-half.
tossups.r: Its namesake won the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physics for it. For 10 points, name this rule saying each orbital holds at most two electrons, which must have opposite spins.

tossups.p: Because of this principle, an atom’s nth electron shell can hold at most 2n² electrons, so the second shell can hold eight and the third can hold eighteen. This principle forces lithium’s third electron into the second shell, since the first shell is already full.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantum rule, stated by an Austrian-born physicist in 1925, that keeps two electrons in an atom from sharing the same state.

tossups.p: Because photons do not obey this principle, huge numbers of them can share one state in a laser beam. In orbital diagrams, this principle is the reason that the two arrows drawn in one box must point in opposite directions, one up and one down.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle, which says no two electrons in an atom have the same four quantum numbers.

tossups.p: Because of this principle, a p subshell can hold at most six electrons and a d subshell at most ten. Chemistry students use this principle along with Hund’s rule and the Aufbau [“OWF-bow”] principle when they write electron configurations.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle that forces two electrons in the same orbital to have opposite spins.

tossups.p: Five years after stating this principle, its namesake proposed a tiny neutral particle, later named the neutrino, in a 1930 letter that began “Dear Radioactive Ladies and Gentlemen.” Electron “degeneracy pressure” caused by this principle keeps white dwarf stars from collapsing.
tossups.r: Because of it, electrons fill atoms shell by shell. For 10 points, name this rule saying no two electrons in an atom can have exactly the same quantum numbers.

tossups.p: Atoms in a Bose–Einstein condensate can all pile into the same lowest-energy state because they are bosons, which ignore this principle. Particles that must obey this principle, such as electrons, protons, and neutrons, are named for Enrico Fermi.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle stating that no two identical fermions can be in the same quantum state at once.

tossups.p: Neon’s ten electrons exactly fill its first two shells, two in the first and eight in the second, because of this principle. This principle also helps explain why the first row of the periodic table has only two elements, hydrogen and helium.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle that says each atomic orbital can hold only two electrons, with opposite spins.

tossups.p: A neutron star only about 20 kilometers across is kept from collapsing into a black hole partly because its neutrons resist being squeezed into the same states, a “degeneracy pressure” that comes from this principle. In atoms, this principle forces electrons into higher and higher shells as more of them are added.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle stating that no two electrons in an atom can have the same four quantum numbers.

tossups.p: In 1926, Enrico Fermi and Paul Dirac independently worked out the statistics that describe large groups of particles obeying this principle. Electrons, protons, and neutrons all obey this principle because they have half-integer spin.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle stating that two electrons in an atom can never share the same set of four quantum numbers.

tossups.p: This principle’s namesake spent most of World War II at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey, and won the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering it. This principle explains why the two electrons in a helium atom’s lowest orbital must have opposite spins.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle stating that no two electrons in an atom can share all four quantum numbers.

tossups.p: The s block of the periodic table is two columns wide and the p block is six columns wide because of this principle, which limits how many electrons each subshell can hold. In covalent bonds, this principle requires the two shared electrons to have opposite spins.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rule, stated in 1925, which says no two electrons in an atom can have the same four quantum numbers.

trap.title: Exclusion, not uncertainty
trap.body: Two famous quantum “principles” get mixed up all the time. This one is about crowding: no two electrons in an atom can share all four quantum numbers. Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle is about measuring: you cannot know a particle’s exact position and exact momentum at the same time. Hund’s rule and the Aufbau principle are separate electron-filling rules that also have their own answer lines.
trap.fix: Opposite spins, two electrons per orbital, quantum numbers, fermions, or white dwarfs mean this principle. Position, momentum, h-bar, or Heisenberg means the uncertainty principle, and electrons spreading out into empty orbitals before pairing up means Hund’s rule.
trap.line: Real answer line: Pauli exclusion principle (accept exclusion principle or Pauli principle; prompt on Pauli; do not accept “uncertainty principle”)
